title: provider (plugin)
objectives: Pick the right provider variant (Provider vs ChangeNotifierProvider vs ProxyProvider vs StreamProvider)

sections.markdown:
**Think of `provider` as the office intercom system.**

Every widget in the tree is a room in a building. `provider` mounts an **intercom (`InheritedWidget`)** at some level of the tree. Rooms below can:

- **Listen** (`context.watch<Counter>()`) — the intercom pages this room every time `Counter` changes. Room repaints.
- **Ask once** (`context.read<Counter>()`) — this room dials the intercom, gets the value, doesn't subscribe. No rebuild on change.
- **Filter** (`context.select<Cart, int>((c) => c.itemCount)`) — the intercom only pages when the *itemCount slice* changes; ignores unrelated `Cart` field changes.

A `ChangeNotifierProvider` is the intercom that holds a `ChangeNotifier`; whenever it fires `notifyListeners()`, subscribed rooms rebuild.

**Why `provider` shaped a generation of Flutter code:** before it, DI + state exposure required either global singletons (untestable) or drilling props through 5 constructors (`prop drilling`). `InheritedWidget` was the built-in answer, but its API was awkward. `provider` wrapped `InheritedWidget` in an ergonomic API, added lifetime management (`dispose` called automatically), and paired with `ChangeNotifier` gave Flutter its first great state-management story. Riverpod, Bloc, and MobX all take inspiration from it. Even in 2026, half of Flutter tutorials + the majority of small/mid apps still use `provider` because it's simple + battle-tested.

**`provider`** (`^6.1.x`) is Remi Rousselet's dependency-injection + state-observation library built on Flutter's `InheritedWidget`. Ships variants: `Provider<T>` (immutable value), `ChangeNotifierProvider<T>` (mutable observable), `ValueListenableProvider`, `StreamProvider`, `FutureProvider`, `ProxyProvider` (derived from other providers), and `MultiProvider` (composition). Consumers use `Provider.of<T>(context)`, extension methods `context.read/watch/select`, or the `Consumer<T>` builder widget. Automatic `dispose` when the provider leaves the tree. **Predecessor + inspiration for Riverpod**, still recommended in the Flutter docs for small/mid apps.

## The three access APIs — watch vs read vs select
## Common mistakes
**Mistake 1: `context.watch` inside `initState`.** InheritedWidgets aren't ready until `didChangeDependencies`. Use `context.read` in `initState`, or move logic to `didChangeDependencies`.

**Mistake 2: `context.watch` inside a callback (`onPressed`).** Callbacks aren't in the build phase — `watch` throws `ProviderNotFoundException` or produces stale reads. Use `context.read` in callbacks.
**Mistake 3: `notifyListeners()` inside `build`.** Infinite rebuild loop — flutter throws 'setState during build.' Only mutate + notify in event handlers / futures.
**Mistake 4: One giant VM for the whole app.** Every field change rebuilds every consumer. Split into focused VMs (`CartVM`, `AuthVM`, `ThemeVM`) or use `select` to filter.

**Mistake 5: Provider without `.value` when you already own the object.** `ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: existing)` when the object outlives the widget; use `create:` when the provider should own the lifetime + call `dispose`.
**Mistake 6: Nested Consumer soup.** Three deep Consumers = three rebuild scopes crossing. Combine with `Selector` or move to `context.select` inside the outer widget.

**Mistake 7: `provider` above `MaterialApp` for i18n / theme.** Routes navigate to new pages that don't inherit the same tree unless you provide above `MaterialApp` (or via `builder`). Understand the tree.
**Mistake 8: Testing without `ChangeNotifierProvider` wrap.** Widget tests need the provider in scope; use `pumpWidget(ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => TestVM(), child: SUT()))`.
## Best practices
**1. `read` in callbacks, `watch` in build, `select` for slices.** Rule memorized.
**2. Focused VMs.** One per screen or feature, not one god VM.
**3. `MultiProvider` for app-level DI** — repositories, API clients, config.
**4. `ProxyProvider` for derived state** — recompose when a dependency changes.
**5. `StreamProvider` / `FutureProvider` for external sources** — Firebase snapshots, one-shot fetches.
**6. `Selector` around expensive widgets** — limit rebuild scope.
**7. Widget tests wrap with the necessary provider tree** — verify observability.
**8. Move to Riverpod** if you outgrow provider: compile-time safety, no BuildContext dependency, better async.
## Practice programs
**Practice 1 (Easy)** — Counter with `ChangeNotifierProvider` + `context.watch`.
**Practice 2 (Medium)** — Split into `CounterVM` + `ThemeVM`; use `select` for theme so counter changes don't rebuild theme.
**Practice 3 (Medium)** — `ProxyProvider` — build `UserRepository` from `ApiClient`.
**Practice 4 (Hard)** — `StreamProvider` on a Firestore snapshot; UI reacts live.
**Practice 5 (Hard)** — Diagnose a rebuild storm using Flutter DevTools; fix with `Selector`.
**Practice 6 (Expert)** — Widget test that pumps a `ChangeNotifierProvider` + verifies UI observability.
## Interview Q&A

**Q1: `watch` vs `read` vs `select` — when do you use each?**

**A:** **`watch<T>()`** — subscribes the current `build` method to any change of `T`. Use in `build`. Rebuilds the widget whenever `T.notifyListeners()` fires. **`read<T>()`** — one-shot read, no subscription. Use in `initState`, `onPressed`, `Future.microtask`, anywhere OUTSIDE the build phase. Cheap. **`select<T, R>((t) => t.someSlice)`** — subscribes only to the slice `R`; the widget rebuilds only when the slice changes, ignoring unrelated T changes. Use when a widget cares about a subset of a big VM (e.g., only `Cart.itemCount`, not full `Cart`). Rule to memorize: **read in callbacks, watch in build, select for slices.** Violating this either crashes (`watch` in callback) or produces rebuild storms (`watch` when `select` would do).

**Q2: What's the underlying Flutter mechanism?**

**A:** `provider` is a thin wrapper around **`InheritedWidget`**. When you write `ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => VM(), child: ...)`, it mounts a `_InheritedProviderScope<VM>` in the tree. Descendant widgets that call `context.watch<VM>()` register themselves as dependents via `dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType`. When the `ChangeNotifier` fires `notifyListeners`, provider iterates registered dependents and marks them dirty for rebuild. `read` uses `getElementForInheritedWidgetOfExactType` — reads without subscribing. `select` layers on top: it subscribes but re-evaluates the selector; if `oldSlice == newSlice`, no rebuild. **Consequence:** everything provider does is standard Flutter mechanism — no runtime magic, testable via `pumpWidget`, works with hot reload. **Not exclusive to `ChangeNotifier`** — any observable (Stream, ValueListenable, Future) has its own Provider variant.

**Q3: You have a screen that rebuilds too often — how do you diagnose + fix?**

**A:** **Diagnose:** enable Flutter DevTools's **Repaint Rainbow** or **`debugPrintRebuildDirtyWidgets`** — the widgets that flash on every state change are the offenders. **Common patterns:** **(1) `context.watch<BigVM>()` at the top of the widget** subscribes to any change, so *every* field change rebuilds the entire subtree. Fix: `context.select<BigVM, R>((vm) => vm.smallField)` for each place. **(2) Anonymous callbacks in build (`onPressed: () => ...`)** — technically not a rebuild issue but keeps identity stable across rebuilds; less common cause. **(3) Nested Consumers of unrelated VMs** — split into `Selector` widgets that watch narrow slices. **(4) Multi-purpose `ChangeNotifier`** — refactor into small focused VMs. **(5) `StreamProvider` re-emitting the same value** — override equality on the emitted class. **Metric that matters:** frame time. p50 < 16ms; if not, Repaint-Rainbow + Timeline profile.

**Q4: When would you migrate from `provider` to Riverpod?**

**A:** Migrate when you hit these pain points: **(1) `ProviderNotFoundException` at runtime** — provider is BuildContext-scoped; forgetting to wrap something is a compile-passing runtime error. Riverpod checks at compile time. **(2) Async initialization is awkward** — `FutureProvider` + errors is verbose; Riverpod's `AsyncValue` is nicer. **(3) `ProxyProvider` composition explodes** — 4 layers of derived state = unreadable soup; Riverpod's family + ref.watch is cleaner. **(4) Testing without BuildContext** — Riverpod runs providers in pure Dart tests. **(5) Family / autoDispose semantics** — provider has no first-class support; Riverpod does. **Cost:** rewrite of the state-management layer. **Migration path:** identify screen-scoped VMs first (easy wins), leave root-level DI on provider (also easy to move but low priority), test-cover as you go. **When NOT to migrate:** small stable app, team knows provider well, no acute pain — churn is expensive.

**Q5: How do you handle async data with provider?**

**A:** Options: **(1) `FutureProvider<T>`** — one-shot fetch; children see `AsyncSnapshot`-like states via `context.watch<AsyncSnapshot<T>>()` (or a builder). Cleans up when leaving tree. **(2) `StreamProvider<T>`** — continuous updates (Firestore snapshot, WebSocket). Same builder-style consumption. **(3) `ChangeNotifierProvider` + manual future in the VM** — VM holds `loading/data/error` fields, calls the future, notifies. Most flexible; verbose. **(4) `flutter_bloc` / Riverpod** — better ergonomics for complex flows. **Trap:** kicking off a fetch inside `build` — will re-fetch on every rebuild. Do it in `initState` (with `context.read`) or in VM constructor with a load flag. **Recommendation:** `FutureProvider` for simple one-shots; VM pattern for anything with retries, refresh, or user-triggered mutations.

**Q6: What are common testing patterns for provider-backed widgets?**

**A:** **(1) Widget test with `ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => TestVM(), child: SUT())`.** VM instance controlled by the test; fire events + `pump()` + verify. **(2) Fake VMs** — implement the interface with a `TestVM extends ChangeNotifier` that has pre-programmed states. **(3) `Mocktail` for VM methods** — combined with a `.value` provider for injecting the mock. **(4) `MultiProvider` in tests** — mimic the app tree exactly for integration widget tests. **(5) Unit-test the VM in isolation** — no widget tree needed; assert on notifyListeners calls via a `TestListener`. **(6) `ProviderScope` isolation** — each test gets a fresh scope; teardown ensures no state leaks between tests. **Key insight for interviews:** the test *tree* mimics the runtime *tree*; provider makes DI trivial at test time.

## Real-world usage

- **Small + mid Flutter apps** — the reference state-management for years.
- **Firebase snapshots** — StreamProvider around `Firestore.collection().snapshots()`.
- **App-level DI** — repositories, API clients, theme, locale.
- **NOT ideal for** — very large apps with complex derived-state graphs (Riverpod / Bloc win).

## Advanced notes

- **`Provider.debugCheckInvalidValueType`** — hook to guard against passing non-immutable values into `Provider<T>`.
- **`MultiProvider` composition order** — later providers can read earlier ones via `ProxyProvider.update`.
- **`Consumer<A, B, C>`** — multi-consumer for 2-6 providers at once.
- **`Provider.value` vs `Provider(create: ...)`** — value: reuse an outer object; create: provider owns lifetime + calls dispose.
- **`ChangeNotifier` equality** — provider re-emits on `notifyListeners`; if you override `==`, ensure it still matches actual changes.
- **`ValueListenableProvider`** — great for lightweight `ValueNotifier<T>` counters.
- **`StateNotifierProvider`** — from `flutter_state_notifier` — immutable-state-emitting notifier; Riverpod adopted this pattern.
- **Not for global state?** — provider is scoped by widget tree; there is no default 'app-wide singleton' concept, though `MultiProvider` at root emulates it.
- **Hot reload safety** — `provider` handles hot reload gracefully; if VM state matters, `dispose + create` fresh on reload.
- **Riverpod's genesis** — same author (Remi Rousselet); provider laid the groundwork.
- **Bloc + provider** — many teams provide a Bloc via `BlocProvider` (which is provider-based) alongside app-level providers.
